title: The Copy Trading Starter Guide
subtitle: How to choose, size and follow a strategy without fooling yourself

p: Copy trading lets you link your own broker account to a trader's strategy. When they open a position, your account opens the same one, scaled to your balance. When they close it, yours closes too.

That is all it is. It is not a savings account, and it is not a way to skip learning how risk works. The trader can be wrong, the market can gap, and a good year can follow a bad month. This guide is about going in with your eyes open.

sections.h: 1. How it works on cTrader Copy
p: Your money stays in your account, in your name, at your broker. The strategy provider never touches it. They only send trades.
You can stop copying at any time. Open positions can be closed straight away or left to run, your choice.

Fees are shown before you start. The common one is a performance fee: a share of your net profit, worked out with a high-water mark. That means you only pay on new highs. If the account drops and comes back to where it was, you do not pay twice for the same gain.
Each provider sets a minimum to copy. Below that amount the platform will not let you start.
sections.tip: Check the fee type before anything else. A performance fee only gets paid when you make money. A management or volume fee gets paid either way.

p: Screenshots prove nothing. A verified record is pulled straight from the broker by a third party such as Myfxbook, so nobody can edit it.
Look at four numbers together, never one alone:
list: Gain: the return over the whole period, adjusted for deposits and withdrawals.
Drawdown: the biggest fall from a peak. This is the pain you need to be able to sit through.
Age: three months of results says much less than twelve. Short records can look amazing by luck.
Profit factor: gross profit divided by gross loss. Above 1 means it made more than it lost.
sections.tip: Small accounts produce wild percentages. A 10 dollar loss on a 20 dollar balance is minus 50 percent. Check the balance behind the number.

p: Start with money you can lose without changing your life. Not money for rent, not money you borrowed.

Copying scales by equity: if the provider has 10,000 and you have 1,000, you trade about a tenth of their size. Too small and some trades cannot be copied at all, because the broker has a minimum lot size.
Give it time. One week tells you nothing. Decide in advance how long you will follow before judging, three months is a sensible floor.

list: Write down the drawdown you can live with, in percent, before you start.
If the account hits it, stop and review. Do not double up to win it back.
Never move money out of a copy account in the middle of open trades. It changes the scaling and can leave positions without margin.
Keep one strategy per copy account so the numbers stay clean.
Review once a month, not every hour.

p: Most of the market for signals runs on the same tricks. Walk away when you see these:
list: Accuracy claims with no verified account behind them.
Profits shown in big dollar amounts, never in percent of the account.
No drawdown anywhere on the page.
Pressure to message an admin in private to get the price.
Lifetime VIP deals that only make sense if you never ask for results.
Accounts that keep changing. A record that restarts often is hiding something.
Is the record verified by a third party?
Has it run for at least three months?
What was the worst drawdown, and could I live with it?
What exactly are the fees, and when are they charged?
What is the minimum, and does my balance clear it comfortably?
Can I stop at any time, with my money in my own name?

p: Every number we publish comes from the live account, verified on Myfxbook. Results are shown in percent, losses included. Days without trades are reported as days without trades.

We never show account balances in dollars, never promise returns and never post buy or sell calls. If you want to see how a strategy behaves before you copy it, follow the channel for a while and judge it yourself.
